Q: How to build a machine learning model to predict football match scores and win/draw/loss probabilities? A:

Very good question. Actually, this problem can be modeled using Survival analysis. To be very specific, you are looking for competing risk estimation.

You can read the paper: DeepPseudo and Federated Competing Risk Analysis.

From DeepPseudo paper, I am providing one sentence describing the competing risk:

Competing Risk Analysis (CRA), an important problem in survival analysis, aims to estimate the probability of occurrence of an event in the presence of competing events.

Modeling approach

  1. You can use the statistics based CoxPH models. Alternatively, deep learning based DeepPseudo models can be used for more accurate risk or probabilities calculation.

  2. To combine score prediction with win/draw/loss probabilities, you have to use time-to-event approaches. Use appropriate evaluation metrics.

**Features: **

  1. You have to preprocess the features. Categorical features can be one-hot encoded.

**Evaluation Metrics: **

  1. You have to use C-Index and Brier Score.

**Existing open-source projects: **

  1. You can check this codebase: https://github.com/umbc-sanjaylab/FedPseudo_KDD23

Hopefully it will help.

Q: Understanding Church numerals A:

There is no x in (lambda (x) x). None.

The x in (lambda (x) x) is bound. It could be named by any name whatever. We can not talk about x in (lambda (x) x) any more than we could talk about x in (lambda (y) y).

There is no y in (lambda (y) y) to speak of. It is just a placeholder, an arbitrary name whose sole purpose in the body is to be the same as in the binder. Same, without regard for which specific name is used there as long as it is used twice -- first time in the binder, and the other time in the body.

And in fact there is this whole 'nother notation for lambda terms, called De Bruijn notation, where the same whole thing is written (lambda 0). With 0 meaning, "I refer to the argument bound by the binder that is 0 steps outside the expression".

So x is unimportant. What's important is (lambda (x) x) which denotes a function which returns its argument as is. The so called "identity" function.

But even this is not important here. The Church encoding of a number is really a binary function, a function expecting two arguments -- the f and the z. The "successor step" unary function f and the "zero" "value" z, whatever that might be, as long as the two go together. Make sense together. Work together.

So how come we see two unary functions there when it is really one binary function in play?

That is the important bit. It is known as currying.

In lambda calculus all functions are unary. And to represent a binary function an unary function is used, such that when given its (first) argument it returns another unary function, which, when given its (now, second) argument, performs whatever thing our intended binary function ought to perform, using those two arguments, the first and the second.

This is all very very simple if we just write it in combinatory (equational) notation instead of the lambda notation:

zero f z = z
one  f z = f z
two  f z = f (f z) = f (one f z)
                   = succ one f z
succ one f z = f (one f z)

where every juxtaposition denotes an application, and all applications associate on the left, so we imagine the above being a shortcut notation for

zero f = ^z. z        ; ^ for λ, lambda
zero = ^f. (^z. z)
     = ^f. ^z. z
     = ^f z. z
......
......
succ = ^one f z. f (one f z)
     = ^one. (^f. (^z. f ((one f) z) ))
;; such that
succ one f z = (((succ one) f) z)
  = ((( (^one_. (^f_. (^z_. f_ ((one_ f_) z_) ))) one) f) z)
  = ((          (^f_. (^z_. f_ ((one  f_) z_) ))       f) z)
  = (                 (^z_. f  ((one  f ) z_) )           z)
  =  f (one f z)

but it's the same thing. The differences in notation are not important.

And of course there is no one in ^one f z. f (one f z). It is bound. It could just be named, I dunno, number:

succ number f z = f (number f z) = f ((number f) z)

meaning, (succ number) is such a number, that, given the f and the z, does one more f step compared to what number would do.

And so, ((zero square) 100) means, use the number zero with the successor step square and the zero value of 100, and have zero perform its number of successor steps for us -- that is to say, 0 steps -- starting from the zero value of 100. Thus returning it unchanged.

Another possible use is ((zero (lambda (x) 1)) 0), or in general

((lambda (n) ((n (lambda (x) 1)) 0)) zero)  

;; or even more generally, abstracting away the 0 and the 1,

((((lambda (n) (lambda (t) (lambda (f) 
     ((n (lambda (x) f)) t)))) 
          zero)         0)          1)

which is just another way of writing

zero (^x. 1) 0            ; ... or,

foo n t f = n (^x. f) t   ; and calling:

foo zero 0 1

Hopefully you can see what foo is, easily, how it returns the t value if n is zero and f otherwise. And also how to read aloud this t and this f. (Probably the original f would be better named s then, or something like that, as a mnemonic for "successor", to not clash with this use).

Another example is the predecessor function,

pair a b h = h a b        ; h for 'handler'
first  p = p (^a b. a)
second p = p (^a b. b)
pred n s z 
   = second (n (^p. pair (succ (first p))
                         (first p)) 
               (pair zero zero))
            s z
   = second (n (^p. pair (s (first p))
                         (first p)) 
               (pair z z))
   = n (^p. p (^a b h. 
            h (s a) a))   ; advance and repackage
       (^h. h z z)        ; initial pair
       (^a b. b)          ; final result handler
   = n (^r a b. r b 
                  (s b))  ; advance and continue
       (^a b. a)          ; final result handler
       z z                ; initial pair
   = n (^r a b. a 
                 (r b b)) 
       (^a b. z)
       I s

Such that, ultimately,

I x = x

n      s z = s (s (s (... (s z) ...)))
pred n s z =    s (s (... (s z) ...))
           = I (s (s (... (s z) ...)))
           = X (X (X (... (X Z) ...))) I
           = n (^r a. a (r s)) (^a. z) I   ;;; <<-------
           = I (X (X (... (X Z) ...)) s) 
           = I (s (X (... (X Z) ...) s)) 
           = I (s (s((... (X Z) ...)s))) 
           = ..... 
           = I (s (s (... (s (Z s)) ...)))

using Church numerals' (lazy) right fold to encode the passing of an accumulator from left to right (i.e., from the top down). The "accumulating", here, being the switching from I to s after the first use. The iterated "step" function, X, being immutable as everything is in lambda calculus, the only way to modify its behavior is by passing an additional argument to it, while modifying it along the way.

Q: NASM bootloader: Protected mode jump to kernel at 0x00010000 shows nothing in VirtualBox A:

Stack relocation

init_stack:
    cli
    mov ax, 0x0000
    mov ss, ax
    mov sp, 0x9C00
    sti
    ret

You can't relocate the stack in a called subroutine and then return, because your return address is on the old stack. You'll need to add some code to retrieve it before switching, or else simply put this routine in line in the caller.

Also, this code should be run before loading the kernel (BootNucleus). AFAIK, the BIOS doesn't make any promises about where the stack is located at boot, except that it normally points to a reasonable amount of usable memory. So in principle it might be located in the region where you are going to load the kernel, which would overwrite it.

Segment registers

    lgdt [gdt_descriptor]

DS is still set to 0x1000 after your BootNucleus routine. (Which itself was unnecessary, because the INT 0x13 BIOS call only requires the segment of the buffer in ES.) But with org 0x7c00, all accesses to static data require a segment of 0. You do have SS = 0 at this point so you could do lgdt [ss:gdt_descriptor], but it's probably cleaner to just reset DS. (Keep in mind that although many BIOSes will set it to 0 before jumping to your boot code, this is not guaranteed, and other BIOSes may leave it with a different value.)

Interrupts

You left interrupts enabled after init_stack, which is fine as long as you stay in real mode; the interrupt vector table and stack are still valid. But once in protected mode, when an interrupt arrives, the machine will look to the interrupt descriptor table (IDT) to find the handler. You haven't set up an IDT, so this will result in a triple fault (since the exception resulting from the invalid IDT also can't be handled, for the same reason). This causes the machine to reset and you have a "boot loop".

So you should disable interrupts (cli) before switching to protected mode.

(Technically it isn't necessary to disable interrupts to move the stack, as long as you load SS and SP with consecutive instructions in that order; x86 has a feature where interrupts are automatically disabled for one instruction after loading SS. But it's probably a good habit anyway.)

After fixing these issues, your code works successfully for me in Bochs. I did not try with VirtualBox, though.

I’m not sure whether jumping directly to 0x00010000 is correct, or whether I should jump to the label Nucleus instead.

Jumping to 0x00010000 is fine and correct, since that matches the address where you loaded the kernel. (You might want to use equ to give it a symbolic name, in case you want to change it someday, and compute the segment and offset passed to int 0x13 from it.) It won't work to use the label Nucleus which is defined in the kernel file, since you're assembling the kernel separately, and copying it as a binary image rather than actually linking them together.

Q: Struct with dynamically allocated array that works on host and device with Cuda A:

How could I get this to work?

(This is not the only possible approach, but...)

I would be guided by two principles:

  1. Separate your concerns.
  2. Don't reinvent the wheel... although some wheels in C++ were invented crooked and may merit a redesign.

I am assuming your dynamic allocation is made on the host side only. Dynamic allocation on the device side is usually a bad idea and slows you down massively.

Given that assumption, the reasonable kind of class to exchange between host and device side is a span: Take a well-regarded implementation, and adapt it to GPU use by marking the methods as __host__ __device__. If you're using C++20 or later and allow CUDA to user constexpr host-side code on the device side, you can use std::span directly, but - NVCC's support for using constexpr is experimental, and may have undesirable side-effects, so even though it's a more handy solution, it may be a bit risky.

Now, on the host side, I will make the further assumption that you don't frequently re-allocate, so that you don't need an std::vector like class in which an emplace_back() may reallocate. So, you would be looking for something like the never-actually adopted std::dynarray; except that standard library allocators are crap, and PMR is an ugly band-aid over them. So, you could go with a non-std dynarray and PMR allocators which in turn either use new, or cuHostAlloc(), or cuMemAalloc() etc - or you could do partial-wheel-reinvention: A class which is like unique_ptr, but also holds the size and allows use as if it were a span.

I've done that myself for my CUDA API wrapper library: my unique_span<T> class). And it is, in fact, a "work-horse" in many of my adapted CUDA samples, such as vectorAdd.

(If you feel this answer is a bit too hand-wavy, please say so and I'll elaborate on one or more aspects of it.)

Q: Pillow installation PyPy3 missing zlib A:

Installing using UV

For those using uv package manager, struggling with the build on windows and those who don't want to fiddle with funny flags and parameters (or can't), please just:

  1. install vcpkg

  2. install the c/c++ header files using vcpkg install zlib libjpeg-turbo

  3. add environment variables to your windows environment either by running

    $env:INCLUDE = "C:\\vcpkg\\installed\\x64-windows\\include;" + $env:INCLUDE 
$env:LIB = "C:\\vcpkg\\installed\\x64-windows\\lib;" + $env:LIB

    or by adding the paths to the respective variables manually using the GUI in Windows

  4. run uv add pillow or uv add pillow-simd, both should work now.
